headline: Massachusetts generic-drug settlement case expands as consumers face March claim deadline
dek: New agreements with Ascend, Mayne and Citron add to a multistate antitrust case; Massachusetts buyers should check the covered-drug list and distinguish deadlines before filing.
body: Massachusetts consumers who bought certain generic prescription drugs between May 2009 and December 2019 may be eligible for compensation as a multistate antitrust case adds three more proposed settlements. The Massachusetts Attorney General’s Office said Oct. 8 that it had joined other state and territorial attorneys general in asking a federal court to approve agreements involving Ascend Laboratories, Citron Pharma and Mayne Pharma. The states allege that the manufacturers participated in a long-running effort to inflate prices, reduce competition and restrain trade. Those allegations remain claims in litigation, not findings that every company or drug involved violated the law.

The proposed agreements have different financial terms. Ascend would pay $400,000 to the multistate coalition, while Mayne would pay $650,000, according to the Massachusetts attorney general’s release. Citron’s agreement contains no monetary payment because the company has ceased operations, the office said. All three companies also agreed to internal reforms described as injunctive relief, including measures intended to strengthen competition-law compliance. The court must still review and approve the agreements before they become final.

The Oct. 8 announcement is part of a larger case rather than a new lawsuit limited to Massachusetts. The attorney general’s office said earlier settlements with Sandoz, Glenmark, Lannett, Bausch, Apotex, Heritage Pharmaceuticals and Heritage’s parent, Emcure, total $496.5 million. The [official settlement site](https://www.aggenericdrugs.com/English/Home?portalid=0) says the litigation continues against manufacturers that have not settled and that any distribution will follow court-approved plans. That means the new agreements add to an evolving pool of settlements; they do not establish a guaranteed payment for every person who purchased a generic drug.

Eligibility depends on the specific medicine, purchase dates and other requirements in the settlement materials. Consumers should use the covered-drug list and claim instructions rather than assume that a prescription or a pharmacy purchase automatically qualifies. The claims administrator says people seeking payment must submit a signed, valid claim form; it also says receipts are not required for one filing option, although documentation may later be requested to support an estimated out-of-pocket amount. The administrator, not a pharmacy or the Massachusetts attorney general, makes the eligibility determination.

The deadlines also require care because the settlements are moving on separate tracks. The claims site currently lists March 8, 2027, as the deadline for an initial distribution tied to the Glenmark settlement. It separately lists the deadline for the newer Ascend, Citron and Mayne group as not yet determined. Consumers should check the site for the settlement that covers the drug they purchased and should not treat the March date as a universal deadline for every agreement. The site lists online and mail filing options as well as a toll-free number, 1-866-290-0182.

The case has a direct New England connection beyond Massachusetts because the state coalition includes the region’s other attorneys general. The [Maine attorney general’s announcement](https://www11.maine.gov/ag/news-and-library/press-releases/attorney-general-aaron-m-frey-seeks-court-approval-settlements) said the states are preparing for the first trial in Hartford, Connecticut, in February 2027. That trial date concerns claims against non-settling defendants and is separate from the court’s review of the proposed settlements. It also shows why the consumer process and the underlying litigation should not be treated as the same event.

For Massachusetts residents, the practical question is whether a listed generic medicine was purchased during the covered period, not whether the buyer lives in a particular city or used a particular pharmacy. The attorney general’s office urged consumers to review the settlement information and determine eligibility through the claims administrator. The [New York attorney general’s account](https://ur.ag.ny.gov/press-release/2026/attorney-general-james-secures-over-1-million-ascend-laboratories-and-mayne) independently describes the same Ascend and Mayne agreements and the March 8, 2027, claims date used for the broader process.

The next major legal step is court review. The settlement site lists a Nov. 5, 2026, final-approval hearing for the Glenmark agreement, while the newer Ascend, Citron and Mayne materials still show several dates as pending. Until approval and the allocation process are complete, the eventual amount any eligible consumer could receive is unknown. Residents considering a claim should rely on the current court and settlement notices, keep a record of what they submit and avoid paying anyone to file a claim on their behalf.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Massachusetts generic-drug settlement claims and deadlines
seoDescription: New generic-drug settlements add to a multistate case involving Massachusetts buyers. Here is what is known about eligibility, deadlines and court review.
